claim: Spinster-RFP localizes to an expansive tubular network in Drosophila muscle.
source: Remarkably, when Spinster-RFP is expressed in Drosophila muscle, Spin-RFP localizes to an expansive tubular network (Figure 1A–C and Video 1).
evidence: Directly observed through live imaging of fluorescently tagged Spinster protein in muscle tissue, with supporting figures and video.

claim: Tubules are found evenly distributed throughout the sarcoplasm and form a web of connections with other tubules.
source: Tubules were found evenly distributed throughout the sarcoplasm and formed a web of connections with other tubules (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Observed through microscopy imaging showing distribution pattern.

claim: Enlarged vesicular compartments are observed at tubule intersections throughout the muscle.
source: We also observed enlarged vesicular compartments at tubule intersections throughout the muscle (Figure 1C).
evidence: Direct observation from imaging data.

claim: The tubular network is highly sensitive to chemical fixation conditions.
source: This network is highly sensitive to all chemical fixation conditions that we have attempted.
evidence: Experimental observation across multiple fixation attempts.

claim: When subjected to fixation, the tubule lattice collapses, leaving behind distributed round, Spinster-positive compartments.
source: When subjected to fixation, the tubule lattice collapses (Figure 1D), leaving behind distributed round, Spinster-positive compartments that resemble classically defined late-endosomal, lysosomal structures (Sweeney and Davis, 2002; Dermaut et al., 2005).
evidence: Observed morphological change upon fixation, with reference to prior characterization of these structures.

claim: Live imaging is essential to study the function and relevance of the Spin-positive tubular network.
source: Thus, live imaging is essential to study the function and relevance of this Spin-positive, tubular network.
evidence: Logical conclusion based on the observation that fixation destroys the network structure.

claim: The tubular network exhibits evidence of tubule extension, retraction, scission and fusion.
source: We next explored the dynamics of this tubular network in time-lapse videos. We find evidence of tubule extension, retraction, scission and fusion (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: Direct observation from time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: The dominant activity in the network is the dynamic extension and retraction of individual tubules throughout the sarcoplasm.
source: The dominant activity in the network is the dynamic extension and retraction of individual tubules throughout the sarcoplasm (Figure 1E and Video 2).
evidence: Observed as the most frequent activity in time-lapse videos.

claim: Scission events from the end of a tubule result in a mobile vesicle.
source: In less frequent instances, we observed scission events from the end of a tubule, resulting in a mobile vesicle (Figure 1F).
evidence: Direct observation from time-lapse imaging.

claim: Tubule extensions can result in tubules fusing to larger nodes in the network.
source: In a corollary phenomenon, we observed tubule extensions that resulted in tubules fusing to larger nodes in the network (Figure 1G).
evidence: Direct observation from time-lapse imaging.

claim: De novo formation of tubules can extrude from the side of existing tubules.
source: Finally, we observed de novo formation of tubules extruding from the side of existing tubules (Figure 1G, last panel) demonstrating that tubulation can originate from existing tubules, not just pre-existing nodes.
evidence: Direct observation from imaging with interpretation of mechanism.

claim: An identical, dynamic tubular lysosomal network exists in intact larvae imaged through the cuticle.
source: Importantly, the existence of a tubular network and tubule dynamics are not an artifact of a dissected neuromuscular preparation. We observed an identical, dynamic tubular lysosomal network in intact larvae that were imaged through the cuticle while restrained in a microfluidics chamber (Video 3).
evidence: Direct observation in intact animals confirms the network is not an artifact of dissection.

claim: Treatment with nocodazole for 1 hr completely abolished tubules.
source: Treatment with nocodazole for 1 hr completely abolished tubules, indicating that the tubules require microtubule support (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Experimental manipulation with microtubule-disrupting drug.

claim: The tubules require microtubule support.
source: Treatment with nocodazole for 1 hr completely abolished tubules, indicating that the tubules require microtubule support (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Inferred from the effect of nocodazole treatment.

claim: Disruption of the actin cytoskeleton with latrunculin A did not have a significant effect on the tubular network.
source: In contrast, disruption of the actin cytoskeleton with latrunculin A did not have a significant effect on the tubular network, indicating a non-essential role for the actin cytoskeleton in maintaining lysosome tubules (Figure 1J).
evidence: Experimental manipulation with actin-disrupting drug.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton has a non-essential role in maintaining lysosome tubules.
source: In contrast, disruption of the actin cytoskeleton with latrunculin A did not have a significant effect on the tubular network, indicating a non-essential role for the actin cytoskeleton in maintaining lysosome tubules (Figure 1J).
evidence: Inferred from lack of effect of latrunculin A treatment.

claim: Expression of Clathrin heavy chain RNAi completely disrupted network integrity.
source: Expression of Clathrin heavy chain RNAi (Chc-RNAi) completely disrupted network integrity (Figure 1K).
evidence: Experimental manipulation through RNAi knockdown.

claim: Spinster was characterized previously as a lysosomal marker.
source: Although Spinster was characterized previously as a lysosomal marker, the tubular structures labeled by Spinster are dramatically different from the classical view of vesicular lysosomes.
evidence: Reference to prior characterization work.

claim: Spin-GFP completely co-localizes with the low pH fluorescent probe Lysotracker.
source: First, we co-imaged Spin-GFP with the low pH fluorescent probe Lysotracker and found complete co-localization (Figure 2A), indicating that the Spinster network is acidic.
evidence: Co-localization experiment with pH-sensitive dye.

claim: The Spinster network is acidic.
source: First, we co-imaged Spin-GFP with the low pH fluorescent probe Lysotracker and found complete co-localization (Figure 2A), indicating that the Spinster network is acidic.
evidence: Inferred from co-localization with Lysotracker, which labels acidic compartments.

claim: Lysotracker staining confirmed the existence of the tubular network in wild type muscle.
source: To verify that the observed tubular network is not an artifact of Spin-RFP over-expression, we stained wild type muscles with Lysotracker to examine lysosome morphology under wild type conditions. Lysotracker staining confirmed the existence of this tubular network in wild type muscle (Figure 2B).
evidence: Staining of endogenous structures without overexpression of markers.

claim: Tubule intersections stained more intensely for Lysotracker than the tubules themselves.
source: We also note that the tubule intersections stained more intensely for Lysotracker than the tubules themselves.
evidence: Observation from imaging data.

claim: Spin-RFP tubules do not co-localize with ER or mitochondria tubules.
source: ER and mitochondria also form tubule structures, but when we co-imaged Spin-RFP with ER-tracker and Mito-tracker fluorescent dyes, Spin-RFP tubules did not co-localize with either ER or mitochondria tubules (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Co-localization experiments with organelle-specific markers.

claim: Spin-RFP tubules are interwoven between mitochondria and ER tubules.
source: Instead, Spin-RFP tubules were interwoven between mitochondria and ER tubules.
evidence: Spatial relationship observed in imaging data.

claim: Spin-RFP does not co-localize with markers for early endosomes, recycling endosomes, medial Golgi or trans Golgi.
source: Additionally, Spin-RFP did not co-localize with markers for early endosomes (YFP-Rab5), recycling endosomes (Rab11-GFP), medial Golgi (ManII-GFP) or trans Golgi (GalT-YFP) (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: Co-localization experiments with multiple organelle markers.

claim: Golgi organization in muscles forms vesicular structures rather than the classical Golgi stacks.
source: We note that Golgi organization in muscles forms vesicular structures rather than the classical Golgi stacks that are observed in most cell types and this is consistent with Golgi organization that has been observed in vertebrate skeletal muscles (Ralston et al., 2001).
evidence: Observation from imaging data, consistent with prior literature.

claim: A dynamic tubular lysosomal network permeates the entire sarcoplasm of Drosophila body-wall muscle in vivo.
source: Collectively, we have identified and characterized a dynamic tubular lysosomal network that permeates the entire sarcoplasm of Drosophila body-wall muscle in vivo.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Inhibiting VCP expression by RNAi abolished lysosome tubules, leaving behind vesicles throughout the sarcoplasm.
source: Specifically, inhibiting VCP expression by RNAi abolished lysosome tubules, leaving behind vesicles throughout the sarcoplasm (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Experimental manipulation through RNAi knockdown with imaging.

claim: The lysosome vesicles in VCP RNAi muscles are irregular in their size and shape and appear clustered.
source: The lysosome vesicles were irregular in their size and shape and appeared clustered, rather than uniformly distributed throughout the sarcoplasm.
evidence: Morphological observation from imaging.

claim: Acute inhibition of VCP with DBeQ completely disrupted the tubular network after 3 hr.
source: To determine whether the catalytic ATPase function of VCP is required for the tubular network integrity, we employed a VCP-selective inhibitor DBeQ (Chou et al., 2011). Acute inhibition of VCP with DBeQ completely disrupted the tubular network after 3 hr (Figure 3C,D), demonstrating the required catalytic function of VCP.
evidence: Pharmacological inhibition experiment with specific VCP inhibitor.

claim: The catalytic ATPase function of VCP is required for tubular network integrity.
source: To determine whether the catalytic ATPase function of VCP is required for the tubular network integrity, we employed a VCP-selective inhibitor DBeQ (Chou et al., 2011). Acute inhibition of VCP with DBeQ completely disrupted the tubular network after 3 hr (Figure 3C,D), demonstrating the required catalytic function of VCP.
evidence: Inferred from the effect of catalytic inhibitor DBeQ.

claim: After treatment with DBeQ for 4 hr, the remaining vesicular lysosome structures are completely static.
source: Furthermore, time-lapse imaging of Spin-GFP after treatment with DBeQ for 4 hr revealed that the remaining vesicular lysosome structures are completely static (Video 4).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging after drug treatment.

claim: Over-expressing human VCP in dVCPRNAi muscles rescued the formation of lysosome tubules in every muscle.
source: Over-expressing human VCP in dVCPRNAi muscles rescued the formation of lysosome tubules in every muscle (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: Genetic rescue experiment with human ortholog.

claim: VCP knockdown is the cause of disrupted lysosomal network integrity.
source: These rescue data confirm that VCP knockdown is the cause of disrupted lysosomal network integrity and demonstrate that VCP-dependent activity is conserved in the human VCP protein.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiment results.

claim: VCP-dependent activity is conserved in the human VCP protein.
source: These rescue data confirm that VCP knockdown is the cause of disrupted lysosomal network integrity and demonstrate that VCP-dependent activity is conserved in the human VCP protein.
evidence: Demonstrated by functional rescue with human VCP.

claim: Expression of parkin-RNAi and tbph-RNAi did not have a significant effect on lysosome tubules.
source: Remarkably, we did not observe any significant effect on lysosome tubules (Figure 3H–J) when parkin-RNAi and tbph-RNAi are expressed with BG57-Gal4, the same Gal4 line used to express VCP-RNAi throughout our studies.
evidence: Comparison experiments with other degenerative disease-related genes.

claim: Upon treatment with tunicamycin for 4 hr, the Spin-RFP tubular network remained intact.
source: To address this possibility, we treated muscles with tunicamycin (TM) to induce ER stress by another means and examined the tubular network. Upon treatment with TM for 4 hr, the Spin-RFP tubular network remained intact (Figure 3K,L).
evidence: Experimental manipulation to induce ER stress through alternative mechanism.

claim: Total protein levels of Hsc70/BiP were significantly increased in both TM and DBeQ treated muscles.
source: We verified that ER stress was induced by examining levels of Hsc70/BiP, a marker of ER stress, in protein lysates derived from the same animals that were used for imaging. Total protein levels of Hsc70/BiP were significantly increased in both TM and DBeQ treated muscles (Figure 3M).
evidence: Western blot analysis of ER stress marker.

claim: Tubular network disruption is not a byproduct of ER stress.
source: Thus, tubular network disruption is not a byproduct of ER stress.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ER stress induced by tunicamycin does not disrupt tubules.

claim: VCP loss of function disrupts the integrity of the tubular lysosomal network.
source: Taken together, our data are consistent with three conclusions: (1) VCP loss of function disrupts the integrity of the tubular lysosomal network, (2) the role of VCP in maintaining tubular lysosomes is conserved and (3) disruption of the tubular network is specific for VCP loss of function and not a secondary byproduct of muscle degeneration or ER stress.
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: The role of VCP in maintaining tubular lysosomes is conserved.
source: Taken together, our data are consistent with three conclusions: (1) VCP loss of function disrupts the integrity of the tubular lysosomal network, (2) the role of VCP in maintaining tubular lysosomes is conserved and (3) disruption of the tubular network is specific for VCP loss of function and not a secondary byproduct of muscle degeneration or ER stress.
evidence: Demonstrated by human VCP rescue experiment.

claim: Disruption of the tubular network is specific for VCP loss of function and not a secondary byproduct of muscle degeneration or ER stress.
source: Taken together, our data are consistent with three conclusions: (1) VCP loss of function disrupts the integrity of the tubular lysosomal network, (2) the role of VCP in maintaining tubular lysosomes is conserved and (3) disruption of the tubular network is specific for VCP loss of function and not a secondary byproduct of muscle degeneration or ER stress.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with other degenerative conditions and ER stress induction.

claim: mCherry-Atg8a precisely co-localizes with Spin-GFP-labeled tubules.
source: Remarkably, we find that mCherry-Atg8a precisely co-localizes with Spin-GFP-labeled tubules (Figure 4A).
evidence: Co-localization experiment with autophagosome marker.

claim: The mCherry-Atg8a labeling is widely distributed within the network, but does not label the full extent of every tubule.
source: The mCherry-Atg8a labeling is widely distributed within the network, but does not label the full extent of every tubule (Figure 4A).
evidence: Observation from co-localization imaging.

claim: mCherry-Atg8a labeling is dynamic within Spin-GFP tubules.
source: Time-lapse imaging revealed mCherry-Atg8a labeling is dynamic within Spin-GFP tubules (Video 5).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging showing movement over time.

claim: Some mCherry-Atg8a puncta appear to traffic through the Spin-GFP tubules.
source: Some mCherry-Atg8a puncta appear to traffic through the Spin-GFP tubules suggesting that autophagosome membranes and/or cargos are dynamic within the tubular lysosome network (Figure 4B).
evidence: Observation from time-lapse imaging.

claim: The mCherry-Atg8a positive regions of the lysosome tubules represent ongoing degradation of autophagosome membranes following fusion with the Spin-GFP positive lysosomal network.
source: Given this sequence of events, we propose that the mCherry-Atg8a positive regions of the lysosome tubules represent ongoing degradation of autophagosome membranes following fusion with the Spin-GFP positive lysosomal network.
evidence: Interpretation based on known autophagy biology and observed co-localization.

claim: When VCP was knocked down, Atg8 no longer co-localized with Spin-GFP.
source: Next, we explored the consequence of disrupting VCP activity on Atg8 and Spin-GFP co-localization. When VCP was knocked down and the tubular-lysosomal network was eliminated, Atg8 no longer co-localized with Spin-GFP (Figure 4C).
evidence: Observation from imaging after VCP knockdown.

claim: Atg8-positive vesicles are found closely apposed to Spin-positive, vesicular lysosomal compartments in VCP knockdown.
source: Rather, Atg8-positive vesicles were found closely apposed to Spin-positive, vesicular lysosomal compartments.
evidence: Spatial relationship observed in imaging after VCP knockdown.

claim: The close apposition of autophagosomes and lysosomes in VCP knockdown suggests that autophagosomes can identify and potentially dock against lysosomal membranes, but fusion is defective.
source: This close apposition suggests that the autophagosomes can identify and potentially dock against the lysosomal membranes, but fusion of the autophagosome with the lysosome is defective.
evidence: Interpretation of the observed spatial relationship.

claim: The yeast VCP homolog, Cdc48, has an established role in membrane fusion.
source: This is consistent with an established role for the yeast VCP homolog, Cdc48, in membrane fusion (Latterich et al., 1995).
evidence: Reference to prior literature on yeast homolog function.

claim: When GFP-mCherry-Atg8a was expressed in muscles, no detectable GFP fluorescence was found in the tubules that label strongly for mCherry-Atg8a.
source: When we expressed the dual fluorescence reporter in muscles we found no detectable GFP fluorescence in the tubules that label strongly for mCherry-Atg8a (Figure 4D), consistent with other data indicating that the tubules are acidic.
evidence: Observation using pH-sensitive dual fluorescence reporter.

claim: Upon treatment with concanamycin A for 3 hr, GFP and mCherry positive tubules were observed.
source: To further test the acidic nature of the tubules, we treated muscles with concanamycin A, a specific inhibitor of the lysosomal V-ATPase that is required for lysosome acidification (Huss et al., 2002). Upon treatment with ConA for 3 hr, we observed GFP and mCherry positive tubules (Figure 4E).
evidence: Experimental manipulation with V-ATPase inhibitor.

claim: The lysosome tubules are acidic.
source: Together, these data further verify that the lysosome tubules are acidic and also demonstrate that acidification is not necessary to maintain the structure of the tubules.
evidence: Conclusion from dual fluorescence reporter and V-ATPase inhibitor experiments.

claim: Acidification is not necessary to maintain the structure of the tubules.
source: Together, these data further verify that the lysosome tubules are acidic and also demonstrate that acidification is not necessary to maintain the structure of the tubules.
evidence: Inferred from observation that tubules remain intact after V-ATPase inhibition.

claim: Inhibiting VCP function with DBeQ created GFP-positive vesicles.
source: Again, we explored the consequence of disrupting VCP activity. Inhibiting VCP function with DBeQ created GFP-positive vesicles (Figure 4F) that must be non-acidified compartments, a finding that is consistent with the existence of autophagosomes that have not yet fused with Spin-positive lysosomes.
evidence: Observation using dual fluorescence reporter after VCP inhibition.

claim: The GFP-positive vesicles after DBeQ treatment are non-acidified compartments consistent with autophagosomes that have not yet fused with lysosomes.
source: Inhibiting VCP function with DBeQ created GFP-positive vesicles (Figure 4F) that must be non-acidified compartments, a finding that is consistent with the existence of autophagosomes that have not yet fused with Spin-positive lysosomes.
evidence: Interpretation based on pH-sensitive reporter behavior.

claim: There is a continual flux of material through the auto-lysosomal system in muscle cells at steady state.
source: Since the appearance of GFP-positive vesicles occurs in a time frame of minutes to hours, it suggests that there is a continual flux of material through the auto-lysosomal system in muscle cells at steady state.
evidence: Inferred from the rapid appearance of unfused autophagosomes after VCP inhibition.

claim: Expression of Atg7-RNAi did not affect lysosome tubules.
source: Finally, we examined whether autophagy influx was required to induce or maintain lysosome tubules. Expression of Atg7-RNAi, an RNAi line that has been shown previously to inhibit autophagosome assembly (Ren et al., 2009), did not affect lysosome tubules (Figure 4G).
evidence: Experimental manipulation blocking autophagosome formation.

claim: Autophagy induction is not a prerequisite for lysosome tubules.
source: Thus, autophagy induction is not a prerequisite for lysosome tubules.
evidence: Inferred from lack of effect of blocking autophagosome assembly.

claim: Loss of VCP disrupts the fusion of autophagosomes with functional lysosomes.
source: To this point, our data suggest that loss of VCP disrupts the fusion of autophagosomes with functional lysosomes and, in parallel, causes the collapse of the tubular lysosomal network.
evidence: Summary interpretation of multiple experimental results.

claim: Loss of VCP causes the collapse of the tubular lysosomal network.
source: To this point, our data suggest that loss of VCP disrupts the fusion of autophagosomes with functional lysosomes and, in parallel, causes the collapse of the tubular lysosomal network.
evidence: Summary of experimental observations.

claim: VCP confirms previous reports that VCP is required for autophagosome-lysosome fusion.
source: Taken together, these data confirm previous reports that VCP is required for autophagosome-lysosome fusion (Tresse et al., 2010b) and further suggest that VCP loss abrogates autophagosome-lysosome fusion by affecting the structural properties of lysosomes.
evidence: Experimental results consistent with prior literature.

claim: VCP loss abrogates autophagosome-lysosome fusion by affecting the structural properties of lysosomes.
source: Taken together, these data confirm previous reports that VCP is required for autophagosome-lysosome fusion (Tresse et al., 2010b) and further suggest that VCP loss abrogates autophagosome-lysosome fusion by affecting the structural properties of lysosomes.
evidence: Interpretation connecting structural and functional observations.

claim: VCP-Venus localizes abundantly in and around the nucleus and diffusely in the cytoplasm.
source: Similar to previous reports for mammalian VCP, we observed abundant VCP localization in and around the nucleus and diffusely in the cytoplasm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation from fluorescently tagged VCP in live muscle.

claim: VCP-Venus concentrates at structures that are labeled by either Spin-RFP or mCherry-Atg8a.
source: But, VCP-Venus also concentrated at structures that are labeled by either Spin-RFP (Figure 5A) or mCherry-Atg8a (Figure 5B), demonstrating that VCP localizes to auto-lysosomes.
evidence: Co-localization experiments with lysosomal and autophagosomal markers.

claim: VCP localizes to auto-lysosomes.
source: But, VCP-Venus also concentrated at structures that are labeled by either Spin-RFP (Figure 5A) or mCherry-Atg8a (Figure 5B), demonstrating that VCP localizes to auto-lysosomes.
evidence: Inferred from co-localization with autolysosomal markers.

claim: Inhibiting VCP activity with DBeQ for 2 hr triggered the formation of rod-shaped VCP aggregates.
source: Surprisingly, inhibiting VCP activity with DBeQ for 2 hr triggered the formation of rod-shaped VCP aggregates that effectively sequester VCP-Venus from the sarcoplasm (Figure 5C).
evidence: Observation after pharmacological inhibition.

claim: When the proteasome inhibitor MG132 was applied, VCP-Venus rapidly aggregated in a manner identical to that observed following DBeQ incubation.
source: Remarkably, when we applied the proteasome inhibitor MG132, VCP-Venus rapidly aggregated in a manner identical to that observed following DBeQ incubation (Figure 5D).
evidence: Observation after proteasome inhibition.

claim: VCP aggregation was not due to increased VCP protein levels as a result of proteasome inhibition.
source: VCP aggregation was not due to increased VCP protein levels as a result of proteasome inhibition, because total VCP protein did not increase significantly upon MG132 or DBeQ treatment (Figure 5E).
evidence: Western blot analysis of total VCP levels.

claim: Application of MG132 induced VCP-Venus aggregate formation, which correlated with dissolution of the tubular lysosomal network.
source: Application of MG132 induced VCP-Venus aggregate formation, which correlated with dissolution of the tubular lysosomal network (Figure 5D).
evidence: Observation of concurrent changes after MG132 treatment.

claim: When MG132 was washed out, VCP aggregates dissolved within 20 min and cytoplasmic VCP fluorescence intensity increased.
source: When MG132 was washed out, VCP aggregates dissolved within 20 min and, as they disappeared, cytoplasmic VCP fluorescence intensity increased (Figure 5F and Video 6).
evidence: Time-lapse observation after drug washout.

claim: During MG132 washout, cytoplasmic VCP-Venus accumulated at autophagosomes/lysosomes and tubules began to reform.
source: During this time, cytoplasmic VCP-Venus accumulated at autophagosomes/lysosomes (mCherry-Atg8a) and tubules began to reform (Figure 5F and Video 6).
evidence: Time-lapse observation showing sequential events.

claim: VCP localizes to auto-lysosomes, where it could participate in auto-lysosomes tubulation.
source: These data indicate that VCP localizes to auto-lysosomes, where it could participate in auto-lysosomes tubulation.
evidence: Interpretation based on localization and washout experiments.

claim: When VCP RNAi was expressed specifically in muscle, muscle wasting was apparent and third instar larvae exhibited a severe impairment in their ability to move.
source: When VCP RNAi was expressed specifically in muscle, muscle wasting was apparent and third instar larvae exhibited a severe impairment in their ability to move (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Behavioral and morphological observation after VCP knockdown.

claim: The defect in motility of VCP RNAi larvae is not due to defects in the nervous system because synaptic transmission at the NMJ remained intact.
source: The defect in their motility is not due to defects in the nervous system because synaptic transmission at the NMJ remained intact (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Electrophysiological measurements of synaptic function.

claim: The impaired muscle function in VCP RNAi is consistent with compromised muscle function that parallels the muscle weakness observed in human VCP-related diseases.
source: These data are consistent with compromised muscle function that parallels the muscle weakness observed in human VCP-related diseases.
evidence: Comparison to known human disease phenotypes.

claim: The enlarged Spin-GFP vesicles in VCP-RNAi muscles co-stain with Lysotracker, indicating that they are acidic.
source: We first examined the acidification of the lysosomes by co-imaging Spin-GFP with Lysotracker in VCP-RNAi animals and found that the enlarged Spin-GFP vesicles also co-stained with Lysotracker (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), indicating that they are acidic.
evidence: Co-localization with pH-sensitive dye.

claim: There is no significant difference in Cathepsin-L processing in VCP-RNAi animals or animals treated with DBeQ.
source: To further examine the functionality of the lysosomes, we examined processing of Cathepsin-L and found no significant difference in Cathepsin-L processing in VCP-RNAi animals or animals treated with DBeQ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Western blot analysis of enzyme processing.

claim: Disruption of the tubular lysosomal network does not appear to affect the proteolytic capacity of sarcoplasmic lysosomes.
source: Thus, disruption of the tubular lysosomal network does not appear to affect the proteolytic capacity of sarcoplasmic lysosomes.
evidence: Inferred from normal Cathepsin-L processing and acidification.

claim: In muscles expressing VCP-RNAi, there is a dramatic accumulation of cytoplasmic poly-ubiquitin aggregates.
source: In wild type muscles stained with a poly-ubiquitin antibody, we observed small puncta around the nucleus and a few small puncta in the cytoplasm (Figure 6A). These small puncta likely represent active sites of protein degradation by the proteasome. However, in muscles expressing VCP-RNAi we observed a dramatic accumulation of cytoplasmic poly-ubiquitin aggregates (Figure 6B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence staining for poly-ubiquitin.

claim: Acute treatment with DBeQ was sufficient to produce cytoplasmic poly-ubiquitin aggregates.
source: Even acute treatment with DBeQ was sufficient to produce cytoplasmic poly-ubiquitin aggregates (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence after pharmacological inhibition.

claim: VCP inhibition caused a dramatic decrease in poly-ubiquitin conjugates around the nucleus.
source: We also note that VCP inhibition caused a dramatic decrease in poly-ubiquitin conjugates around the nucleus, which likely reflects failed delivery of poly-ubiquitinated proteins to the proteasome.
evidence: Observation from immunofluorescence staining.

claim: Spin-positive lysosomes are devoid of poly-ubiquitin staining.
source: Importantly, we find that Spin-positive lysosomes are devoid of poly-ubiquitin staining (Figure 6F), an observation that is consistent with our model of failed fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes.
evidence: Co-imaging of lysosomal marker and poly-ubiquitin.

claim: Muscles expressing VCP-RNAi displayed less mitotracker-Orange CM-H2TMRos staining.
source: Muscles expressing VCP-RNAi displayed less mitotracker-Orange CM-H2TMRos staining and the visualized mitochondria had an altered morphology, appearing round and dispersed rather than being densely packed, tubular structures (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: Staining with mitochondrial membrane potential-sensitive dye.

claim: The visualized mitochondria in VCP-RNAi muscles had an altered morphology, appearing round and dispersed rather than being densely packed, tubular structures.
source: Muscles expressing VCP-RNAi displayed less mitotracker-Orange CM-H2TMRos staining and the visualized mitochondria had an altered morphology, appearing round and dispersed rather than being densely packed, tubular structures (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: Morphological observation from imaging.

claim: The swollen mitochondria observed in the VCP RNAi expressing muscles are likely defective and should be a prime target for mitophagy-dependent degradation.
source: The swollen mitochondria observed in the VCP RNAi expressing muscles are likely defective and should be a prime target for mitophagy-dependent degradation.
evidence: Interpretation based on mitochondrial morphology and known biology.

claim: There is an accumulation of lipofuscin granules in VCP-RNAi expressing muscles.
source: Finally, we noted an accumulation of lipofuscin granules in VCP-RNAi expressing muscles.
evidence: Observation of autofluorescent material.

claim: Lipofuscin granules exhibit auto-fluorescence at 488 nm.
source: A distinguishing property of lipofuscin granules is that they exhibit auto-fluorescence at 488 nm.
evidence: Known property of lipofuscin material.

claim: Strong auto-fluorescent puncta in VCP-RNAi co-localized with LysoTracker, indicative of lipofuscin granules.
source: The wild type muscles did not display any detectable auto-fluorescence at 488 nm (Figure 6I). But, we observed strong auto-fluorescent puncta in VCP-RNAi that co-localized with LysoTracker (Figure 6J), indicative of lipofuscin granules.
evidence: Autofluorescence imaging with lysosomal marker co-localization.

claim: Autofluorescent puncta were not observed to the same extent when wild type muscles were treated with DBeQ for 4 hr.
source: We did not observe autofluorescent puncta to the same extent when wild type muscles were treated with DBeQ for 4 hr (Figure 6K), suggesting that lipofuscin accumulation is a progressive phenotype.
evidence: Comparison of acute vs chronic VCP loss.

claim: Lipofuscin accumulation is a progressive phenotype.
source: We did not observe autofluorescent puncta to the same extent when wild type muscles were treated with DBeQ for 4 hr (Figure 6K), suggesting that lipofuscin accumulation is a progressive phenotype.
evidence: Inferred from difference between acute and chronic VCP loss.

claim: Maintaining the structural integrity of lysosome tubules is critical for lysosome function.
source: These data suggest that maintaining the structural integrity of lysosome tubules is critical for lysosome function.
evidence: Interpretation based on accumulation of degradation substrates.

claim: Over-expression of wild type dVCP does not alter tubular lysosomes.
source: As a control, we show that over-expression of wild type dVCP does not alter tubular lysosomes (Figure 7B).
evidence: Control experiment for disease mutant overexpression.

claim: Over-expression of each of the mutant VCP transgenes (R155H, R191Q, A232E) profoundly impairs the tubular lysosomal network.
source: We then demonstrate that over-expression of each of the mutant VCP transgenes profoundly impairs the tubular lysosomal network (Figure 7C–F).
evidence: Imaging after overexpression of disease-associated mutants.

claim: There is an increase in sarcoplasmic auto-fluorescence when VCP mutants are over-expressed.
source: In parallel, we find an increase in sarcoplasmic auto-fluorescence when these VCP mutants are over-expressed (Figure 7B–G).
evidence: Autofluorescence imaging after mutant overexpression.

claim: Overexpression of the A229E mutation caused the largest increase in auto-fluorescence compared to the other clinical mutations.
source: Overexpression of the A229E mutation, which is the most severe clinical mutation, caused the largest increase in auto-fluorescence compared to the other clinical mutations (Figure 7F).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of autofluorescence across mutants.

claim: The disease mutations are dominant interfering mutations.
source: Because over-expression of the disease relevant VCP transgenes phenocopies VCP-RNAi expression, these data suggest that the disease mutations are dominant interfering mutations.
evidence: Inferred from similarity of phenotypes between overexpression and knockdown.

claim: Overexpression of VCP disease-associated mutations disrupts lysosome tubules in vivo.
source: Thus, overexpression of VCP disease-associated mutations disrupts lysosome tubules in vivo, an effect that causes accumulation of cytoplasmic lipofuscin granules.
evidence: Summary of experimental observations with disease mutants.

claim: Overexpression of VCP disease-associated mutations causes accumulation of cytoplasmic lipofuscin granules.
source: Thus, overexpression of VCP disease-associated mutations disrupts lysosome tubules in vivo, an effect that causes accumulation of cytoplasmic lipofuscin granules.
evidence: Observed correlation between tubule disruption and lipofuscin accumulation.

claim: Lysosomes form a dynamic, tubular array that extends throughout the sarcoplasm of Drosophila muscle, in vivo.
source: Here we demonstrate that lysosomes form a dynamic, tubular array that extends throughout the sarcoplasm of Drosophila muscle, in vivo.
evidence: Summary statement of primary finding.

claim: This is the first observation of such an extensive, dynamic tubular lysosomal network in any in vivo system.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first observation of such an extensive, dynamic tubular lysosomal network in any in vivo system.
evidence: Claim of novelty based on literature knowledge.

claim: VCP is required for the integrity and dynamics of the tubular lysosomal network.
source: We find that VCP is required for the integrity and dynamics of this tubular network.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings with VCP manipulation.

claim: The catalytic activity of VCP is continuously required to sustain network integrity.
source: We provide evidence that the catalytic activity of VCP is continuously required to sustain network integrity.
evidence: Demonstrated by acute inhibitor experiments.

claim: When VCP is depleted or inhibited, the lysosomal network collapses and both cellular proteostasis and autophagy are compromised.
source: When VCP is depleted or inhibited, the lysosomal network collapses and both cellular proteostasis and autophagy are compromised.
evidence: Summary of multiple experimental observations.

claim: Collapse of the network correlates with cellular manifestations of VCP-associated degenerative diseases, including the appearance of protein inclusion bodies.
source: Collapse of the network correlates with cellular manifestations of VCP-associated degenerative diseases, including the appearance of protein inclusion bodies (Kimonis et al., 2008; Weihl et al., 2009).
evidence: Correlation with known disease phenotypes from literature.

claim: Tubular lysosome dysfunction following overexpression of pathogenic VCP mutants represents one the earliest markers of VCP-dependent muscle pathology.
source: While many questions remain unanswered, our discovery of tubular lysosome dysfunction following overexpression of pathogenic VCP mutants represents one the earliest markers of VCP-dependent muscle pathology.
evidence: Interpretation of the significance of findings.

claim: In most tissues, autophagy is induced upon nutrient starvation, but muscles are one of the unique tissues in which autophagy occurs in the absence of starvation.
source: In most tissues, autophagy is induced upon nutrient starvation, but muscles are one of the unique tissues in which autophagy occurs in the absence of starvation (Mizushima et al., 2004).
evidence: Established knowledge from literature.

claim: Basal autophagy is required to maintain muscle mass.
source: In fact, basal autophagy is required to maintain muscle mass (Masiero et al., 2009).
evidence: Established knowledge from literature.

claim: The extended, lysosomal network maintained by VCP is a cellular solution to ensure highly efficient autophagy throughout the entirety of muscle sarcoplasms.
source: We propose that the observed extended, lysosomal network that is maintained by VCP is a cellular solution to ensure highly efficient autophagy throughout the entirety of muscle sarcoplasms.
evidence: Proposed functional interpretation of the observed network.

claim: The lysosomal network could facilitate the local recycling of nutrients throughout the sarcoplasm to effectively meet local demands.
source: Likewise, this network could facilitate the local recycling of nutrients throughout the sarcoplasm to effectively meet local demands.
evidence: Speculative functional interpretation.

claim: VCP is critical for the rapid degradation of muscle proteins during muscle atrophy.
source: In support of this, VCP is critical for the rapid degradation of muscle proteins during muscle atrophy and expression of a dominant negative form of VCP reduces protein degradation by both proteasomes and lysosomes (Piccirillo and Goldberg, 2012).
evidence: Supporting evidence from literature.

claim: The extended, dynamic lysosomal tubule network may be related to autophagic lysosome reformation (ALR).
source: It is possible that the extended, dynamic lysosomal tubule network that we observe is related to ALR, perhaps acting as a platform for efficient ALR throughout the sarcoplasm.
evidence: Speculative connection to known process.

claim: The mammalian Spinster homolog is required for ALR.
source: In support of this, the mammalian Spinster homolog is required for ALR (Rong et al., 2011).
evidence: Supporting evidence from literature.

claim: The tubular network identified in this study more closely resembles the lysosome tubular networks that have been observed in cultured macrophage cells.
source: The tubular network identified in this study more closely resembles the lysosome tubular networks that have been observed in cultured macrophage cells (Swanson et al., 1987a, 1987b; Knapp and Swanson, 1990).
evidence: Comparison to prior observations in literature.

claim: The tubular network may distribute auto-lysosomal activity throughout the cell.
source: We have now identified specific defects associated with loss of lysosome tubules and our data suggest that the tubular network may distribute auto-lysosomal activity throughout the cell.
evidence: Interpretation based on experimental findings.

claim: VCP and the yeast homologue Cdc48 have been ascribed many functions within the cell including cell cycle progression, UPS and ERAD protein degradation, mitophagy and classical autophagy.
source: VCP and the yeast homologue Cdc48 have been ascribed many functions within the cell including cell cycle progression (Moir et al., 1982), UPS and ERAD protein degradation (Meyer et al., 2012; Wolf and Stolz, 2012), mitophagy (Taylor and Rutter, 2011) and classical autophagy (Ju et al., 2009; Tresse et al., 2010a; Dargemont and Ossareh-Nazari, 2012; Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: Summary of established functions from literature.

claim: VCP achieves diverse activities through its generalized function as an ubiquitin-dependent 'segregase' that dissociates protein conjugates tagged with ubiquitin from protein complexes and organelle membranes.
source: VCP achieves these diverse activities, in part, through its generalized function as an ubiquitin-dependent 'segregase' that dissociates protein conjugates tagged with ubiquitin from protein complexes and organelle membranes (Halawani and Latterich, 2006; Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: Established mechanism from literature.

claim: Different cofactors control VCP localization and function for each process that relies upon VCP activity.
source: For each process that relies upon VCP activity, different cofactors control VCP localization and function (Baek et al., 2013).
evidence: Established knowledge from literature.

claim: VCP acts at the autolysosmal membrane to control autolysosomal dynamics and the progression of autophagic protein clearance.
source: Although we cannot distinguish the role of VCP in the initiation and/or maintenance of lysosome tubules, these data argue that VCP acts at the autolysosmal membrane to control autolysosomal dynamics and the progression of autophagic protein clearance.
evidence: Interpretation based on localization and functional data.

claim: The accumulation of poly-ubiquitin aggregates and lipofuscin granules are a direct consequence of impaired VCP-dependent lysosomal function.
source: If VCP is necessary for normal activity of the autophagy-lysosome system in muscle as our data suggests, then it seems likely that the accumulation of poly-ubiquitin aggregates and lipofuscin granules are a direct consequence of impaired VCP-dependent lysosomal function.
evidence: Logical inference from experimental observations.

claim: Pathogenic VCP transgenes in Drosophila do not appear to disrupt VCP roles in the UPS or ERAD pathways.
source: Importantly, these transgenes in Drosophila do not appear to disrupt VCP roles in the UPS or ERAD pathways, emphasizing the role of impaired autophagy in pathogenic VCP phenotypes (Tresse et al., 2010b; Chang et al., 2011).
evidence: Reference to prior characterization of these transgenes.

claim: Lysosomes are classically viewed as vesicular structures to which cargos are delivered for degradation.
source: Lysosomes are classically viewed as vesicular structures to which cargos are delivered for degradation.
evidence: Statement of established view in the field.

claim: VCP is an AAA-ATPase that, when mutated, causes degenerative diseases of muscle, bone and neurons.
source: The dynamics and integrity of this tubular lysosomal network requires VCP, an AAA-ATPase that, when mutated, causes degenerative diseases of muscle, bone and neurons.
evidence: Established knowledge about VCP and disease.

claim: Human VCP rescues the defects caused by loss of Drosophila VCP.
source: We show that human VCP rescues the defects caused by loss of Drosophila VCP and overexpression of disease relevant VCP transgenes dismantles tubular lysosomes, linking tubular lysosome dysfunction to human VCP-related diseases.
evidence: Experimental rescue with human ortholog.

claim: Overexpression of disease relevant VCP transgenes dismantles tubular lysosomes.
source: We show that human VCP rescues the defects caused by loss of Drosophila VCP and overexpression of disease relevant VCP transgenes dismantles tubular lysosomes, linking tubular lysosome dysfunction to human VCP-related diseases.
evidence: Experimental observation with disease mutants.

claim: Tubular lysosome dysfunction is linked to human VCP-related diseases.
source: We show that human VCP rescues the defects caused by loss of Drosophila VCP and overexpression of disease relevant VCP transgenes dismantles tubular lysosomes, linking tubular lysosome dysfunction to human VCP-related diseases.
evidence: Inference connecting experimental findings to human disease.

claim: Disruption of tubular lysosomes correlates with impaired autophagosome-lysosome fusion, increased cytoplasmic poly-ubiquitin aggregates, lipofuscin material, damaged mitochondria and impaired muscle function.
source: Finally, disruption of tubular lysosomes correlates with impaired autophagosome-lysosome fusion, increased cytoplasmic poly-ubiquitin aggregates, lipofuscin material, damaged mitochondria and impaired muscle function.
evidence: Summary of multiple correlated phenotypes observed experimentally.

claim: VCP sustains sarcoplasmic proteostasis, in part, by controlling the integrity of a dynamic tubular lysosomal network.
source: We propose that VCP sustains sarcoplasmic proteostasis, in part, by controlling the integrity of a dynamic tubular lysosomal network.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings.

claim: VCP is the causative gene for IBMPFD, which encompasses inclusion body myopathy, Paget's disease of the bone and frontotemporal dementia.
source: Valosin-containing protein (VCP), the homologue of yeast Cdc48, is the causative gene for a multisystem degenerative disease that was originally termed IBMPFD to encompass the wide range of debilitating clinical outcomes, including inclusion body myopathy (IBM), Paget's disease of the bone (PDB) and frontotemporal dementia (FD) (Watts et al., 2004).
evidence: Established knowledge from literature.

claim: VCP mutations are associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, spastic paraplegia, scapuloperoneal muscular dystrophy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
source: Recently, the list of degenerative disorders that are associated with VCP mutations has expanded to include amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Abramzon et al., 2012), spastic paraplegia (Clemen et al., 2010), scapuloperoneal muscular dystrophy (Liewluck et al., 2014) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (Gonzalez et al., 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge from literature.

claim: There are currently no viable treatments available to slow or halt progression of VCP-related diseases.
source: Currently, there are no viable treatments available to slow or halt progression of VCP-related diseases.
evidence: Statement of current clinical situation.

claim: Muscle weakness is the first presenting symptom in over 50% of VCP disease patients.
source: Muscle weakness is the first presenting symptom in over 50% of VCP disease patients (Weihl et al., 2009), yet very little is known about the muscle pathology of VCP-related diseases.
evidence: Clinical data from literature.

claim: Muscle biopsies from patients with VCP-related diseases display an accumulation of cytoplasmic poly-ubiquitin aggregates.
source: Muscle biopsies from patients with VCP-related diseases display an accumulation of cytoplasmic poly-ubiquitin aggregates (Watts et al., 2004; Weihl et al., 2009; Dolan et al., 2011), suggesting a major defect in protein clearance.
evidence: Clinical pathology data from literature.

claim: Pathogenic mutations in VCP do not seem to impair the UPS or ERAD protein degradation pathways.
source: But, pathogenic mutations in VCP do not seem to impair the UPS or ERAD protein degradation pathways (Tresse et al., 2010a; Chang et al., 2011).
evidence: Established findings from literature.

claim: Over-expression of VCP mutant transgenes with disease causing mutations leads to an accumulation of autophagosomes.
source: Specifically, over-expression of VCP mutant transgenes with disease causing mutations leads to an accumulation of autophagosomes (Ju et al., 2009; Tresse et al., 2010a), suggesting that VCP functions in processes related to the maturation or fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes.
evidence: Established findings from literature.

claim: Lysosomes are the major cellular degradation sites for clearing damaged proteins and organelles.
source: Lysosomes are the major cellular degradation sites for clearing damaged proteins and organelles.
evidence: Established knowledge about lysosome function.

claim: In certain systems lysosomes have been observed to adopt non-vesicular morphologies.
source: However, in certain systems lysosomes have been observed to adopt non-vesicular morphologies.
evidence: Reference to prior observations in the literature.

claim: In a subset of bone-derived cultured macrophages, lysosomes form abundant, extended tubules that radiate from the cell center.
source: A particularly dramatic example has been observed in a subset of bone-derived cultured macrophages, where lysosomes form abundant, extended tubules that radiate from the cell center and, in some cases, form an interconnected web throughout the cytoplasm (Swanson et al., 1987a; Knapp and Swanson, 1990).
evidence: Prior observations from literature.

claim: Cellular stress, particularly the induction of high levels of autophagy, induces lysosomal membranes to tubulate and undergo scission to produce new vesicular lysosomes, a process referred to as autophagic lysosome reformation (ALR).
source: Additionally, there are examples where cellular stress, particularly the induction of high levels of autophagy, induces lysosomal membranes to tubulate and undergo scission to produce new vesicular lysosomes, a process referred to as autophagic lysosome reformation (ALR) (Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: Established process from literature.

claim: The molecular repertoire of factors required for lysosome tubule formation is virtually unknown.
source: Moreover, the molecular repertoire of factors required for lysosome tubule formation is virtually unknown.
evidence: Statement about gaps in current knowledge.
